paper_title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Escriba-OCR: 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays Tardelli Ronan Coelho Stekel Federal Institute of São Paulo (IFSP), Brazil November 2026 Abstract Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Paleographers call this diplomatic transcription. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this behaviour on BRESSAY, dataset of 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER), and that compares systems with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Because schools need models they can run on their own hardware, we restrict the study to open-weight systems. We evaluate 22 open baselines: 16 general-purpose VLMs from 2B to 400B parameters and five OCR-specialised VLMs, all without task-specific training, and recogniser trained on BRESSAY lines. The best of them, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages. None reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 3978% of the words that are absent from Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words, including general VLMs whose prompt explicitly asks them not to. We then fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting model, Escriba-OCR-1B, reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best zero-shot baseline (95% CI [4.2, 2.9]), with 1.63% CER on the text alone. Under the case-sensitive metric of the ICDAR 2024 BRESSAY competition it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.22.4%). It recovers 77% of illegible deletions and 67% of insertions and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but it still replaces 60% of the likely misspellings with dictionary words. Three training seeds agree to within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page, with CER within 0.1 points of the GPU model. On 40 letters from another handwriting corpus it reads as well as its base model overall (5.1% against 4.9% CER once the base models appended comments are removed), but misreads words that never occur in BRESSAY, such as first-person verbs and proper nouns, more often (40% against 30%); interpolating its weights with the base models recovers about half of this gap and lowers BRESSAY test CER to 2.00%, at the cost of edit-markup recall. teachers review of 96 apparent corrections finds that 45% of the 89 judgeable ones (95% CI 3555%) are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate error preservation. We report what did not reduce normalisation (contrastive decoding against the textonly prior, over-sampling misspelled words, higher input resolution), analyse error types, per-page behaviour and data scaling, and release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Handwritten essays are the norm in Brazilian schools and in the ENEM, the national university-entrance exam, whose essay (redação) millions of students write every year. Automatic transcription would let teachers use digital feedback tools and let researchers study learner writing at scale, and pipelines that score ENEM essays already digitise handwriting with language-model-based OCR followed by text 1 Figure 1: Escriba-OCR-1B against the 22 open baselines on the 199 BRESSAY test pages. (a) Page CER against model size; MoE models are plotted at their total parameter count. Fine-tuning puts the 1B model far below zero-shot VLMs up to 400 times larger, including its own base model. (b) The features of diplomatic transcription, one dot per system. The best zero-shot deletion recall (29%) belongs to Gemma 3 4B at 0.5% precision. HTR-Flor reads ground-truth line crops, so its line structure is not shown. Error preservation, the last row, remains the open problem for every system (8.4). normalisation [38]. For feedback and research, however, clean text is the wrong target. teacher giving spelling feedback needs caza where the student wrote caza, not the corrected casa, and researcher counting orthographic errors needs every one of them. Paleography calls transcription that reproduces document exactly as written diplomatic transcription: original spelling and mistakes, line breaks and end-of-line hyphenation, deletions and insertions. Its opposite is normalised transcription, which corrects and modernises the text. In this paper we use error-preserving transcription for the diplomatic case. Modern VLMs read handwriting remarkably well [7, 16], but they are also strong language models, and strong language models normalise. Recent work shows that VLM-based OCR rewrites perturbed or implausible text toward plausible forms [17, 23, 27], that many handwriting errors of multimodal LLMs come from language priors [46], and that low CER can hide orthographic normalisation [11]. Learner text is where this matters most, because its errors are the signal. To our knowledge, the extent of the problem has not been measured on handwritten learner essays in Portuguese, and no error-preserving recogniser is available for them. Schools also face practical constraint. Student essays are personal data under Brazils data-protection law (LGPD), so transcription system should run on hardware the school controls. We therefore restrict this study to open-weight models, which can be audited, fine-tuned and deployed locally; proprietary APIs are outside its scope. This restriction need not cost quality: on native benchmark of Brazilian Portuguese text embeddings, an openly licensed, self-hostable model reaches the leading tier [40], and we ask whether the same holds for transcription. We study the problem on BRESSAY [33], 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays transcribed with their errors and edit markup, and make four contributions: 1. benchmark for error-preserving transcription that reports page-level CER and WER, error preservation and invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals (4); 2. an evaluation of 22 open baselines, 21 VLMs from 0.8B to 400B parameters used without taskspecific training and trained HTR model, which shows that none reproduces the markup reliably and that the VLMs normalise most misspellings (7); 3. Escriba-OCR-1B, 1B model fine-tuned in 85 minutes that reduces CER by factor of 2.7 relative to the best zero-shot baseline, improves on the best published page-level BRESSAY result under our reconstruction of the competitions metric, reproduces edit markup and runs on single GPU 2 or, quantised, on CPU (Figure 1; 6, 7); 4. an analysis of what helps and why, including error decomposition, per-page behaviour, data scaling, negative results on decoding and sampling remedies, human review showing that the BRESSAY ground truth itself explains almost half of the apparent corrections, and an out-of-domain test on second corpus with weight interpolation as remedy for the vocabulary that fine-tuning narrows (8).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Handwritten text recognition. Line-level CRNN/CTC models such as HTR-Flor [32], trained on benchmarks like IAM [28], were the standard until page-level, segmentation-free models such as DAN [6] and transformer recognisers such as TrOCR [25]. BRESSAY [33] was the basis of an ICDAR 2024 competition [34], won by the PERO system from Brno [19, 21] with 3.77% page CER, and segmentationfree models of the DAN family later reported 2.332.43% in their main results and 2.24% in their best ablation setting [5]. Neto et al. [35] train four line recognisers on BRESSAY with handwriting synthesised by conditional GAN; averaged over the four, line CER on the full training set is about 12% (11.512.2% across their training regimes, and 6.4% for their best model), and they note that none of their models was designed for the edit markup. All of these systems are trained on the BRESSAY training split, and Table 6 compares Escriba with them under the competitions metric. Earlier work by the BRESSAY authors applied language-model spelling correction to HTR output [31], the opposite of our goal, and LHTR.br [39] is another Brazilian Portuguese handwriting dataset. OCR with vision-language models. End-to-end document models [3, 18] and VLM-based OCR systems [8, 9, 36, 41] transcribe whole pages, mostly printed ones, into Markdown, and general VLMs [1, 2, 12] read handwriting when prompted. Zero-shot evaluations of multimodal LLMs on handwriting [4, 7, 16] report strong accuracy on historical and modern documents. growing body of work studies faithfulness: VLMs read or rewrite [23], lean on linguistic crutches [27], lose visual grounding on unusual text [17] and hallucinate plausible words behind low CER [11]. We bring this question to learner writing, where unfaithfulness erases exactly the information users need. Learner handwriting. Gold et al. [14] proposed annotation guidelines for transcripts that retain orthographic features, with double transcription and high agreement. Gold et al. [13] re-transcribed 1,350 pages of German learner writing accordingly and showed that the decoding dictionary strongly affects whether errors survive. Yasin and Zesch [45] study visual error feedback on handwriting, find that neither modular nor end-to-end systems yet reach acceptable quality, and note that recognisers over-correct learner errors. We follow this line for Brazilian Portuguese, measure how modern open VLMs behave, and release model trained for the task.

sections.title: 3 Data
sections.content: BRESSAY [33] contains 1,000 pages of Brazilian Portuguese argumentative essays, one writer per page, collected from online essay platforms and transcribed line by line with the students spelling. Edits are marked as -text- (struck through, legible), -xxx- (struck through, illegible), ##text## and $$text$$ (inserted above or below the line) and @@???@@ (illegible). We use the official page-level splits  (Table 1)  . Three properties of these data shape our results. Pages are cropped to the text, so handwritten line is only about 19 px tall, and OCR-specialised processors such as LightOnOCRs only downscale images, so upscaling is necessary. ALL-CAPS handwriting is transcribed in sentence case, convention that fine-tuned model can learn and prompted model cannot. Finally, the transcriptions themselves contain mistakes, which we quantify in 8.4. sections.title: 4 Benchmark and Metrics
sections.content: For page with reference rp and hypothesis hp, both are first normalised: Unicode NFC, visually identical glyphs merged (curly to straight quotes, to º, dashes to -), whitespace collapsed. The micro-averaged character error rate is then CER = (cid:80) min (cid:0)d(rp, hp), rp(cid:1) rp (cid:80) , (1) where is the Levenshtein distance. Each page is capped at 100% so that single runaway generation, such as repetition loop, cannot dominate the average. We report three variants, all capped: CER (caseinsensitive, markup included, our main metric), CERcase (case-sensitive) and CERtext (case-insensitive, with struck-through and illegible spans removed and insertions unwrapped, which measures reading of the text alone). Markup is parsed line by line, as in BRESSAY, so an unclosed marker in models output affects only its own line. WER is computed in the same way at the word level, without the cap. Handling of student errors. Let be the Hunspell pt-BR dictionary. After rejoining words split across lines and removing markup, reference words that are lowercase-initial, at least three letters long and not in form the set of likely misspellings; the test split has = 496. With word-level Levenshtein alignment a() between reference and hypothesis, we report Pres = {w : a(w) = w} , Corr = {w : a(w) = w, a(w) D} , (2) together with the shares of words misread (replaced by another non-word) and deleted. Conversely, the invented-error rate is the share of reference dictionary words aligned to non-dictionary word. Preservation alone would reward recogniser that misreads everything, so we always report it together with invented errors. approximates the true misspellings: it also contains foreign words, proper nouns and transcription errors, which we quantify in 8.4. With about 2.5 such words per page, preservation has 95% interval of roughly 4 points. Markup and structure. Each marked span is reduced to (type, content) pair, and precision and recall are computed on the multiset intersection of reference and hypothesis pairs per page. Matching ignores position, and for illegible deletions (-xxx-) the content is empty, so for that type we report precision next to recall. Lines is the share of pages whose output has exactly as many non-empty lines as the reference. Significance. We compare systems with paired page-level bootstrap [20]: the 199 test pages are resampled with replacement = 2,000 times, both systems metrics are recomputed on each sample, and we report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the difference . The bootstrap captures variation over pages but not over training runs. sections.title: 5 Systems
sections.content: All baselines are open-weight models evaluated without task-specific training, except HTR-Flor, which we train on BRESSAY. Table 2 summarises their settings. General-purpose VLMs. Thirteen instruction-tuned VLMs are queried through OpenRouter with an error-preserving instruction in Portuguese. The prompt asks the model to copy exactly, to leave spelling, accents, agreement, punctuation and casing uncorrected, to keep line breaks and end-of-line hyphens and to use the BRESSAY markup; the full prompt is released with the code. The models are Gemma 3 4B, 12B and 27B [12], Gemma 4 31B [15], Qwen2.5-VL 72B [2], Qwen3-VL 8B, 30B-A3B and 235B-A22B [1], Qwen3.5 9B and 27B [37], Llama 4 Scout and Maverick [29] and Mistral Small 3.2 [30]. All OpenRouter queries were made in November 2026. OpenRouter routes requests to third-party providers whose quantisation we cannot control; several models were served by two to five providers (Table 13 in the appendix). Three small VLMs, Qwen3.5 2B and 4B and Qwen3-VL 2B, run locally with vLLM [22] and the same prompt. OCR-specialised VLMs. LightOnOCR-3 0.8B, 1B and 4B [41, 42], PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 [8, 47] and GLM-OCR [9] run locally with their native prompts, since they do not follow instructions. Local models decode greedily with repetition penalty of 1.05. These settings matter: without upscaling and the penalty, Qwen3.5 2B looped on 106 of the 199 test pages. HTR. HTR-Flor [32] is trained on the BRESSAY training lines for 60 epochs with the authors code and evaluated on ground-truth line crops, which gives it perfect segmentation, an advantage over page-level systems. Its lines are assembled into pages for scoring. It produced no markup at all, although the training targets contain it; we did not investigate whether the toolkit filters these characters.

sections.content: Table 3 and Figure 1 summarise the test results, and Table 4 gives bootstrap intervals. Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, against 5.60% for the best zero-shot baseline, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B ( = 3.54, [4.19, 2.94]), and 810% for the other strong baselines. The gap is similar on the text alone (1.63% against 4.61%), so it does not come from markup. Two further training runs with different seeds reach 2.05% and 2.03%; over the three seeds, CER is 2.05 0.02, CERtext 1.64 0.02 and error preservation 24.9 1.3 (mean SD). The released model is thus typical of the recipe, and the spread across seeds is about hundredth of the gap to the best baseline. Markup recall varies by at most 2 points across seeds (Table 12 in the appendix). Fine-tuning also teaches the transcription conventions that zero-shot models cannot follow: Escriba recovers 38% of legible deletions, 77% of illegible deletions (with 68% precision) and 67% of insertions, whereas no zero-shot model recovers more than 16% of insertions (Qwen3.5 27B) or any deletions with useful precision. sections.title: 8.1 Where the remaining errors are
sections.content: Table 8 decomposes the character errors. Accents contribute little: stripping all diacritics lowers CER by only 0.070.29 points for every system. Punctuation contributes more, 0.3 points for Escriba and 1.11.5 points for the strongest zero-shot models. The edit counts show the main difference between the fine-tuned model and the baselines: Escribas errors are mostly letter substitutions, with insertions and deletions of similar size, while the zero-shot models make as many deletions as substitutions, because they drop words and whole lines. sections.content: Figure 2a shows the distribution of page CER. Escriba transcribes 30% of the pages with less than 1% CER and 83% with less than 3%, with median of 1.52% and worst page of 8.7%. sections.title: 8.7 Out-of-domain test and weight interpolation
sections.content: Test set. To test Escriba outside BRESSAY, we use the Brazilian Forensic Letter database (BFL) [10], in which 315 writers each copied the same letter, about 130 words long, three times. The letters were scanned at 300 dpi in grey levels, and the text differs from an essay in genre and vocabulary: it is job application written in the first person, with an address block, proper nouns and abbreviations such as V. Sas. and S. A., and many writers use block capitals. We drew one letter from each of 40 writers at random. The author transcribed them in two passes. In the first, he started from the printed text of the letter and corrected it wherever the writer deviated from it, before any model was run; starting from the printed text anchors the reference to it, so deviations he overlooked remain as model errors. In the second, he re-examined 191 points: the 183 at which Escriba and its base model agreed against the reference, and the 8 spans that Escriba marked as deleted or illegible; the review tool showed the competing readings without saying which model produced them. sections.title: 9 Discussion
sections.content: A 1B model fine-tuned for 85 minutes on 647 pages reduces the error of the best zero-shot baseline, 235B mixture-of-experts, by factor of 2.7, and it is the only system in our study that follows the transcription conventions of the corpus. We attribute most of the gain to two ingredients, of which only the second was ablated: an OCR-specialised base model, which already reads as well as general VLMs many times its size, and training the vision encoder on the target handwriting. The result matters for schools in three ways. 1B model runs on single modest GPU or, quantised, on an ordinary CPU, so essays need not leave the institution; teachers care about what students struck out and added, which no zero-shot model reproduces reliably; and following corpuss conventions, such as its casing, is what fine-tuning provides and prompting does not. Error preservation is the open problem. Every model we tested normalises, and fine-tuning reduces this only partly; in the human review, 43% of the words Escriba changed were genuine misspellings that it normalised. On BRESSAY, however, almost half of what looks like normalisation is noise in the reference, so error-preserving benchmarks need adjudicated, double-annotated ground truth [14], and preservation must be read together with the invented-error rate, without which recogniser that misreads everything, such as HTR-Flor, looks faithful. The out-of-domain test shows the other side of the same language prior. Fine-tuned on essays alone, Escriba reads essay vocabulary better than its base model and other vocabulary worse, so that Soube becomes sobre and proper noun becomes common word. model meant for schools will meet letters, summaries and answers to exercises, written in the first person and full of names. Training data from more genres is the direct remedy; weight interpolation with the base model is cheap partial one, but it trades away edit markup, which only the fine-tuning data teach.

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced benchmark for error-preserving transcription of handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays and evaluated 22 open baselines on it. The VLMs among them normalise students misspellings to large extent, and none of the baselines reproduces the edit markup reliably. Escriba-OCR-1B, 1B model fine-tuned in 85 minutes on one GPU, reduces the character error rate of the best zero-shot baseline by factor of 2.7, improves on the best published page-level result on BRESSAY, reproduces edit markup and runs on single GPU or, quantised to 4 bits, on an ordinary CPU. On 40 letters from second corpus it reads as well as its base model once that models appended comments are removed, but misreads words absent from its training data more often, gap that weight interpolation narrows by about half. Future work includes real classroom photos, training data from more genres, adjudicated ground truth and training signals that reward copying what is drawn over what is likely.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The model was trained on single dataset, and our only out-of-domain test is small: 40 letters that copy one fixed text, with few struck-out words, transcribed by single reviewer whose second pass examined only the points where both models agreed against the reference, plus the spans Escriba marked. BRESSAY pages were collected from online platforms, cropped and at low resolution; performance on real classroom photos is untested, and our robustness numbers rely on synthetic degradations. The BRESSAY transcriptions contain errors, and our review covers 96 cases judged by single, non-blind annotator. The error-preservation metric is dictionary-based: it misses agreement errors (as pessoa) and counts foreign words and proper nouns as misspellings. The bootstrap intervals do not include training variance; three seeds of the final configuration suggest that it is small, but three runs are small sample. CPU latency was measured on cloud VM, not on school hardware. Baselines were run under different input sizes and token limits  (Table 2)  , and OpenRouter served several of them from multiple providers with unknown quantisation, which may lower their scores. BRESSAY has been public since 2024, so the evaluated models may have seen its test images. The general VLMs received single error-preserving prompt; we did not test prompt variants or few-shot examples. We fine-tuned single base model, so we cannot say how close another fine-tuned VLM would come. The comparison with published BRESSAY results rests on our reconstruction of the competitions metric, whose scoring script is not public, and on numbers reported by other authors. Finally, the study covers open-weight models only and makes no claim about proprietary systems.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Escriba-OCR-1B transcribes and does not assess, and it should not be used for grading or other highstakes decisions without human review. Because BRESSAY may be used for non-commercial research and teaching only, the model is released under CC BY-NC 4.0. We encourage local deployment so that students essays are not sent to third-party services. The human review was carried out by the author, teacher, on public dataset images.
